Page 28 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program Figure 29: Several possible configurations for the motion control axis of an internally mounted electron beam gun Sensing and Monitoring Capabilities Process monitoring equipment that can be used in electron beam welding includes in-situ measurements (e.g. beam measurement) that occur before welding, and in-operando measurements (e.g. optical or thermal imaging) that occur during welding. Electron beam processes operate in a vacuum, which can damage or decrease the effectiveness of equipment through pressure differentials, lack of convective cooling, or vapor deposition. In- addition, the x-rays produced during the process can damage or decrease the effectiveness of sensors. This requires custom modifications of sensors to operate with electron beam welding. Some vendors have a well-established process development protocol that it has integrated with an advanced qualification approach which is graphically represented in Figure 30. This protocol is currently used to develop the wire-fed electron beam additive manufacture (WEBAM) components but can also be used for welding processes. In-situ measurement with beam characterization equipment enables automated measurement, tracking, and calibration of the electron beam properties (e.g. power, profile, diameter, focus). There are several models of beam characterization equipment available on the market. A fully computerized numerical control (CNC) system enables an automatic control of all relevant parameters for all the mechanical drives, and the electro-magnetic operations of the electron beam. It also provides the collection of this data leading to a repeatable, high quality welds and documentation of the production process. Figure 30: Flow diagram of Pro-Beam's process development protocol including automated beam calibration, process monitoring and recording, to repeatably manufacture a high quality 316L WEBAM component Technologies for online electron-optical (ELO), light optical, and thermal observation allow the monitoring of the melt pool in real time and the recording of the process providing traceability for quality control as shown in Figure 30. Each of these monitoring methods are integrated into the system with closed loop control. On-line ELO using the back scattered electrons created by the electron beam and does not suffer under the vapor deposition of the metal vapor on optical systems.
